description:
Make lunar engineering playable. We want students to understand how power, life support, food, and radiation protection interact, grounded in NASA evidence.

Seeking science, game or web development, design, and education skills. San Francisco, November 14 and 15, 2026. Project work begins at the hackathon.
summary: Lunar Ledger is an interactive browser game that makes lunar engineering trade-offs playable. Students command a four-person outpost through eight shifts, allocating limited power to oxygen generation, water recycling, greenhouse lighting, and science. Changing sunlight, battery reserves, and solar-particle events force players to balance crew survival against a 24-point science objective. Each shift explains how their choices affect the outpost, and a final debrief encourages reflection and replay. NASA resources ground the life-support, plant-growth, radiation-protection, and lunar-environment concepts. Clearly identified teaching assumptions simplify the engineering without presenting the game’s numbers as validated mission predictions.
details:
Lunar Ledger turns the player into the commander of a lunar outpost. Four astronauts must survive eight consecutive shifts while the player works toward a 24-point science objective.

HOW IT WORKS

Players distribute power among oxygen generation, water recycling, greenhouse lighting, and science instruments. Each system competes for the same energy supply. Solar output changes across the mission, while battery storage helps bridge periods without sunlight. Excessive demand creates shortages that affect the systems relying on that power.

During solar-particle events, players choose whether to shelter the crew. Sheltering reduces exposure but also reduces scientific output. This introduces a trade-off between exploration and crew protection.

The game explains resource changes after each shift. Players can inspect the energy balance, identify their resource bottleneck, and replay the scenario with another strategy. Starting plans offer different approaches, including balanced operations, crew protection, and research.

EDUCATIONAL PURPOSE

The intended audience is students learning about space exploration and engineering. The central lesson is that a mission is an interconnected system: conserving power in one area can create a shortage elsewhere. Players learn by making decisions, observing consequences, and explaining what they would change.

The project’s creative focus is making opportunity costs visible through an interactive mission rather than presenting space facts in isolation. Educational effectiveness has not yet been measured through classroom testing.

TOOLS AND IMPLEMENTATION

The game uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and is deployed on Vercel. It runs in the browser without a player account or backend. A separate seven-slide presentation introduces the challenge, controls, trade-offs, and scientific foundations.

NASA RESOURCES AND MODEL LIMITS

NASA resources inform the explanations of integrated life support, water recovery, plant lighting, radiation protection, and the lunar environment. They are listed separately in the NASA Data section and linked within the game.

Power-to-resource rates, crop output, event timing, and radiation-risk scores are simplified teaching assumptions. The game does not reproduce validated astronaut physiology, crop-growth cycles, radiation doses, or actual lunar mission operations. It is an educational model, not a mission-planning tool.

AI ASSISTANCE

OpenAI tools assisted with implementation code. AI assistance is disclosed in the project. NASA has not endorsed or validated the game.
